blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Visual token compaction reduces inference cost by passing only selected image patches or video tokens to later layers. In sequence models with local convolutions, each removal changes which tokens are neighbors. Learning which tokens to keep therefore requires a training signal that accounts for the new neighborhoods. We introduce ProbConv, which computes the exact expected convolution before activation at a kept position under independent keep decisions. The operator is differentiable in the keep probabilities. With binary decisions, ProbConv and step gating reproduce the compacted Mamba block. Across image, vision--language and video backbones, ProbConv is strongest under strong compaction: its advantage over matched training controls grows as more tokens are removed. In Cobra, it also outperforms adaptations of published vision--language pruning methods at matched inference budgets. ProbConv also improves over matched zero-mask training in video frame selection and speech frame dropping. Our code is available at: https://github.com/gmum/probconv
blocks.zh: 视觉符号收缩通过只将所选的图像补丁或视频符号传递到后层来降低推断成本. 在有本地演变的顺序模型中,每个去除符号是邻居的改变. 因此,要学习哪些标志性地保留下来,需要有一个培训信号来说明新的街区。 我们介绍ProbConv, 它计算出确切的预期变化 在启动之前,在一个固定的位置 独立保存的决定。 操作者在保存概率上是不同的. 随着二进制决定,ProbConv和相接相接相接再现了紧凑的曼巴块. 在整个图像、视觉语言和视频主干线上,ProbConv在强力收缩下最强:随着更多的符号被去除,它相对于匹配的训练控制器的优势越来越大。 在"眼镜蛇"中,它也优于所公布的视觉语言穿插方法在相匹配的推论预算上的适应. ProbConv还在视频帧选择和语音帧降下方面改进了匹配的零掩码训练. 我们的代码可在https://github.com/gmum/probconv上查阅。

blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Many image predictions survive the removal of most intermediate patch tokens:
a per-image search on frozen Vision Mamba finds small patch subsets that
preserve the dense prediction [ 73 ] ( Sec. 2 ).
Token compaction aims to learn that choice:
a selector keeps a subset of tokens for each input, and later layers process
the shorter sequence ( Fig. 1 ). The challenge is to learn which tokens remain useful
once those layers operate on the selected subset.

blocks.en:
Removing a token in Mamba changes two computations. The convolutions read
local windows along the token sequence, so closing a gap changes which
tokens fall at each offset. The selective scan also skips the update that
would have occurred at the removed position [ 16 , 11 ] .
Zero masking illustrates the difference: it leaves a slot in the convolution
window and can still update the recurrent state ( Fig. 2 ).

blocks.en:
Token selection methods differ in how they choose and train on masks
( Fig. 3 ). DTP uses an inference-time score without a learned
selector [ 49 ] . DyVM moves sampled survivors into a prefix
during training and uses top- k k at inference [ 64 ] . Its
training and inference masks can therefore differ. OCSampler uses
reinforcement learning (REINFORCE) on compacted clips, with a clip-level reward shared across frame
decisions [ 35 , 63 ] . Straight-through
training with zero masks gives selector gradients through the zero-filled
sequence. Can we train the selector by differentiation, exactly recover
the compacted forward pass for binary masks, and keep the cost linear in
sequence length?

blocks.en:
ProbConv tracks the expected contents of a convolution window as tokens are
kept or dropped. Its gradient compares the windows produced by the two
choices. Step gating lets a dropped position pass the recurrent state
through unchanged and gives the selector a second gradient path. At binary
keep values, the two operations together reproduce the compacted block
( Fig. 1 , top right).
The same construction supports learned token scores and successive
compaction stages ( Sec. 2 ).

blocks.en:
ProbConv is strongest under strong compaction, where removing tokens changes
the neighborhoods of the remaining ones most. In Vim, Cobra and VideoMamba,
its advantage over matched training controls grows as the budget tightens
( Fig. 5 ). In Cobra, it also improves on DTP, FastV and DART adapted
to the same backbone at matched inference budgets [ 49 , 7 , 62 ] ,
and its lead over learned selectors persists at matched training cost. For X3D frame selection, ProbConv trained on sampled
masks matches or exceeds the mean mAP of retrained OCSampler with REINFORCE. In speech, ProbConv improves over matched zero-mask training, while
REINFORCE gives similar or lower word error rates. Compaction speeds up
batched inference in the measured vision setups. Controls that keep the
selector and budget fixed isolate the effect of the training computation,
and ablations show how the convolution gradient and step gating affect
accuracy across backbones. The supplement
covers additional video, genomic and long-context experiments.

Keeping a token inserts it at the front of the window and shifts older
entries back one slot. Dropping it leaves the window in place. Averaging
these updates gives Eq. 4 . Keeping every token ( p t = 1 p_{t}=1 for
all t t ) recovers ordinary convolution. With any binary mask, the window
holds the actual kept predecessors, so the output, with bias and
activation, equals the compacted convolution at every kept position. At fractional p p , the
expectation in Eq. 3 is exact before activation. A centered
convolution, as in X3D-S, is a causal pass plus a causal pass over the
reversed sequence, so ProbConv covers it as well ( Fig. 4 ). The
derivation is in Sec. 4 .

blocks.en: 3 Experiments
blocks.zh: 3 个实验

blocks.en:
We evaluate patch compaction in Vim-Tiny on ImageNet-1k, visual-token
selection in Cobra-3B and spatiotemporal token compaction in VideoMamba-Ti
on Kinetics-400 [ 73 , 52 , 71 , 32 , 27 ] .
We also test frame selection for X3D-S and frame dropping in a Mamba speech
encoder. At inference, each pruned variant processes the physically
compacted sequence. We compare published methods adapted to each setting
and controls that share the selector and budget. In Vim and VideoMamba each
cut keeps a fraction ρ \rho of the remaining patches, as in DynamicViT and
DyVM [ 50 , 64 ] ; Cobra keeps a fraction of the
language-model (LM) FLOPs, as in DTP [ 49 ] ; X3D and speech keep
frames ( Sec. 1 ).

blocks.en: 3.1 Image classification with Vim
blocks.zh: 3.1 国家 带有 Vim 的图像分类

blocks.en:
We train a selector at two cuts in Vim-Tiny, as in ToP-ViM [ 68 ] ,
and fine-tune for three epochs on ImageNet-1k.
On the official validation set, at ρ = 0.3 \rho=0.3 (18 of 196 patches remain),
ProbConv achieves 71.22 % 71.22\% top-1 and the same selector trained
with zero-mask convolution and step gating achieves 66.52 % 66.52\% ( + 4.69 ± 0.56 +4.69\pm 0.56 points, seed-paired). At ToP-ViM’s ρ = 0.8 \rho=0.8 they score 74.72 % 74.72\% and 74.51 % 74.51\% . Across the nine budgets the lead grows from a
tie at ρ = 0.9 \rho=0.9 to 4.7 4.7 points at the tightest ( Fig. 5 a).
DyVM [ 64 ] combines several mechanisms. A ratio loss holds its
Gumbel-sampled predictor near the budget, token distillation from the dense
model recovers accuracy, and block skipping saves further compute. Its
training forward moves the kept tokens ahead of the removed ones, so the scan
reads them as at inference. To isolate how DyVM trains token selection, we keep
our selector, objective and schedule and take only this forward. It scores 0.5 0.5 – 7.0 7.0 points below ProbConv, and the gap grows as budgets tighten
( Main Tabs. 3 and 4 ).

blocks.en: 3.2 Visual-token selection in Cobra
blocks.zh: 3.2 眼镜蛇的可视音箱选择

blocks.en:
We train a visual-token selector before the first language-model block of
frozen Cobra-3B. Baselines include layer-0 Δ \Delta , adaptations of DTP,
FastV and DART, and learned selectors on the same
backbone [ 49 , 7 , 62 ] . As with DTP, FastV and
DART, DyVM enters Cobra as a published method: its predictor trains with its
own objective, alone and with its rearranged forward. The forward gives no gain
at either budget, so Fig. 5 b shows the predictor alone. At 10 % 10\% of LM FLOPs,
ProbConv scores 61.1 61.1 against 58.6 58.6 for layer-0 Δ \Delta , the strongest
training-free rule at that budget ( Tab. 1 ). The gap shrinks
at the milder budget. We use DTP’s best reachable sites at each budget.
DTP leads only at 67 % 67\% of LM FLOPs in the sweep, where its original
pruning sites are reachable.

Against zero masking with step gating, ProbConv ties at 67 % 67\% of LM FLOPs and
leads by 0.3, 0.9, 1.3, 1.9 and 2.7 points at 48, 35, 25, 15 and 10 % 10\% ( Fig. 5 b). The gains on GQA, VQAv2 and POPE
are significant in every seed pair at both main budgets (per-question
tests, Holm correction across benchmarks). VSR and VizWiz stay near their
floors across rules and show no consistent gain.

( Fig. 5 c). As in speech, the zero-mask selector keeps runs of

checkpoint fine-tuned on each split. Averaged over the three splits, ProbConv leads the matched zero-mask control by 1.06 and 1.08 points at ρ = 0.5 \rho=0.5 and 0.7 0.7 , in 17 of 18 seed pairs ( Main Sec. 3.1 ).

blocks.en: 4 Related Work
blocks.zh: 4 相关工作

blocks.en:
Vision transformers shorten sequences by pruning or merging
tokens [ 50 , 8 , 4 ] .
In vision state space models, ToP-ViM aligns hidden states for
retained tokens, DyVM trains a selector by rearranging retained
tokens, and R-MeeTo merges tokens [ 68 , 64 , 57 ] .
Other approaches combine pruning with merging [ 69 , 22 ] or pool and fuse
tokens [ 56 , 48 , 61 , 26 ] .
MTR reduces tokens without training, and STORM preserves the scan’s
spatial structure [ 42 , 41 , 40 ] .
FastV, DART and VTW prune inside the language model, while DTP scores
visual tokens with Mamba’s step size [ 7 , 62 , 37 , 49 ] .
ProbConv gives a selector access to the change in the convolution
window and, with step gating, recovers the compacted block for
binary decisions. As a control, we also train the same selector with
DyVM’s rearranged forward ( Sec. 3.1 ).

Straight-through estimators, continuous relaxations and score-function
estimators provide training signals for discrete choices [ 2 , 25 , 43 , 63 ] .
Differentiable top- k k methods supply keep values at a specified
budget [ 65 , 53 , 59 ] .
Given those keep values, ProbConv specifies the convolution as an
expectation over the changing neighborhoods. Our scan gate applies
the state-skipping principle of Skip RNN [ 6 ] to Mamba’s selective step.

It also supplies a control variate for REINFORCE

the causal smoothing dechunker follows the same rank-one recurrence
as the convolution window ( Main Proposition 1 ).

blocks.en: 5 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 5 结论

blocks.en:
Removing tokens changes what each convolution reads and which steps the
recurrent state takes. ProbConv follows this change exactly in expectation at
linear cost. With step gating it reproduces the compacted Mamba block for
binary decisions, so a selector learns on the network it will deploy. This
matters most at tight budgets. There the advantage over zero-mask training
widens in Vim, Cobra and VideoMamba. In Cobra, ProbConv also outperforms adapted
pruning methods and keeps its lead when learned selectors train for the same
time. X3D frame selection and speech frame dropping show the same advantage
over zero masking, and every gain keeps the inference savings of compaction.
blocks.zh:
删除符号会改变每个音节的读数和步骤
重复状态需要。 ProbConv完全遵循这一变化,预计在
线性成本。 渐渐地复制了紧凑的曼巴块
二进制决定,所以一个选择者在其将要部署的网络上学习. 这个
预算最紧 这比零任务训练有优势
在Vim、Cobra和VideoMamba中扩展。 在眼镜蛇中,ProbConv也优于改编的成绩
运行方法并保持它的领先 当学习的选手训练相同
时间 X3D 帧选择和语音帧下降显示相同优势
并且每个收益都保留了 收缩的推论

blocks.en:
The equivalence with compaction holds only for
binary decisions. ProbConv treats keep decisions as independent, although a
fixed budget couples them, and a joint model could sharpen the training
signal. Training keeps every token in the sequence, so it runs at the dense
length and the savings appear at deployment. Our image and video experiments
use short fine-tuning schedules, and the speed-up depends on batch size and
hardware ( Main Sec. 1.1 ).
blocks.zh:
与压缩的等同性只用于
二进制决定. ProbConv将决定视为独立,尽管

Main Table 1 lists, for every
budget, the tokens kept after each cut, multiply-accumulates
counted analytically and FLOPs in the convention of the compared papers.
For Vim and VideoMamba, the analytic MACs include projections, convolutions,
selective scans in both directions, patch embedding and the head. They exclude
the selector. The Cobra count adds the language-model prefill with 30 text
tokens to the vision backbone and projector, whose cost is measured with
PyTorch’s FLOP counter. The published FLOP figures for Vim and VideoMamba use
the R-MeeTo counter as used by DyVM, which counts one scan direction per block
and includes our selector. For Cobra, DTP’s convention counts the language
model’s prefill MACs with 30 text tokens. At a
fixed ρ \rho the cost does not depend on the method that selects the tokens:
the learned rules (ProbConv, the zero mask, the
straight-through variants) deploy the same network and cost the same; fixed
scores save only the selector, 0.3% of Vim-Tiny’s FLOPs. Rules that prune
inside the network, such as DTP and FastV in Cobra, keep more tokens in early
layers at the same FLOPs, so Cobra’s budgets are matched in FLOPs. In Cobra the
vision backbone and the projector cost 617 GMACs at every budget, against
2,011 GMACs for the dense language model, so 10% of the language-model
FLOPs is 31% of the cost of the whole model.

blocks.en:
We use the Mamba block and convolutional front end of Mamba-based HuBERT [ 36 ] (12 layers of width 384, 17.2M parameters, 50 frames
per second), either causal or with ExtBiMamba layers. The authors released no self-supervised checkpoints, so we train character
CTC [ 14 ] from scratch on LibriSpeech
train-clean-100 [ 47 ] and decode without a language
model. The absolute error rates reflect this 100-hour training setup without
pre-training. All selection rules share the encoder architecture, training
data, optimizer and frame budget. After layer 6 the encoder keeps a fraction ρ \rho of the frames, and
layers 7–12 run on the compacted sequence at inference. An intermediate CTC
head at layer 6 (weight 0.3, [ 31 ] ) provides blank posteriors,
and dropped frames re-enter the final CTC with their layer-6 representation
( Sec. 2.3 ). Baselines select frames with the same budget: uniform
subsampling, CTC top- k k (lowest intermediate blank posterior), and the CTC-peak rule of Soundwave [ 70 ] (CTC spikes first,
then the lowest blank posterior). The selector starts from the intermediate CTC non-blank log-odds and adds the
output of a two-layer MLP on detached layer-6 features. We initialize the
MLP’s last layer at zero, so all learned configurations start from the CTC
top- k k ranking. We train the selector with a zero mask, ProbConv without step
gating, full ProbConv, or ProbConv without the convolution gradient. Models train for 80k steps (AdamW, peak learning rate 5 ⋅ 10 − 4 5{\cdot}10^{-4} , batches of 87.5 s of audio). In the retrofit scenario of
dynamic Vision Mamba pruning [ 64 ] , we instead fine-tune the trained
dense or CTC top- k k model of the same seed for 20k steps with every
selection rule. In a third scenario the dropped frames do not return: the
final CTC reads the compacted sequence and predicts 300 BPE units [ 55 ] learned on the training transcripts. Trained from
scratch, most of these models stayed on the all-blank plateau of CTC, so we fine-tune
the dense character model of the same seed for 40k steps (peak learning rate 10 − 4 10^{-4} ) with a new output head, keeping the character intermediate CTC that
provides the selection prior. We report greedy-decoding WER on test-clean and
test-other.

blocks.en:
We train a one-stage H-Net [ 24 ] for DNA language modeling on
hg38 with the train/validation split of Basenji [ 28 ] :
an encoder and a decoder of two Mamba-2 layers (width 256) around a main network
of six Mamba-2 layers (width 384); 14.8M parameters, contexts of 4096 bases,
20k steps. The published training (“H-Net routing”) uses straight-through
boundaries, the smoothing dechunker and a ratio loss (weight 0.03) towards a
target of N N bases per chunk. In our arms the router is trained through ProbConv and step gating in the main network and the expected dechunker
( Main Proposition 1 ); all models are evaluated with the published hard
forward pass in bits per base on 512 validation windows. To compare at
matched compression we sweep N ∈ { 2 , 3 , 4 , 6 , 8 , 10 } N\in\{2,3,4,6,8,10\} for the published routing
and N ∈ { 2 , 3 , 4 , 6 , 8 , 10 , 12 } N\in\{2,3,4,6,8,10,12\} for our arms, whose routers compress less than
the target, and include an isotropic model of eight Mamba-2 layers without
chunking.

blocks.en:
LDARNet-110M [ 30 ] applies bidirectional dynamic chunking
in front of a BiMamba-2 main network. We fine-tune the released checkpoint on the 18 downstream tasks of the
Nucleotide Transformer benchmark [ 10 ] and reproduce the
authors’ published protocol in full. We run ten-fold cross-validation on the
training split, select the epoch with the best validation MCC and report its
MCC on the fixed test set. We use the published learning-rate schedule and task-specific learning rates,
a batch size of 64, and weight decay of 0.1 on all parameters except biases
and norms. We train for up to 100 epochs and stop after five epochs without an
improvement in validation MCC. The baseline fine-tunes the router with the published
mechanism; our arms train it through ProbConv and step gating in both directions
of the main network and the expected bidirectional dechunker. This amounts to
540 fine-tuning runs (six H100 GPUs for 36 hours). As controls we fine-tune
with the router frozen, add the ratio loss of pre-training ( α = 0.03 \alpha{=}0.03 , N = 4 N{=}4 ) to the fine-tuning objective, and continue the masked language model
pre-training of the released checkpoint on hg38 for 1000 steps of 512
sequences of 4096 bases, with either routing, before the full fine-tuning
protocol.

We start from the released ImageNet-1k Vim-Tiny checkpoint [ 73 ] (BiMamba-v2, 24 blocks of width 192, patch size 16, 224 × 224 224{\times}224 inputs,

blocks.en:
A fixed-size subset couples the keep decisions, whereas ProbConv models them as
independent. The fractional step gate also relaxes the state update. Training
uses the full sequence length. Runtime depends on the operator implementation, host, batch size and hardware.

( Secs. 5 , 2 , 3.1 and 11 ).
The speech and genomics protocols have additional task-specific constraints
( Secs. 6 and 7 ).

Main Table 4 evaluates the
networks of Main Tab. 3 on the 50,000 images of the official ImageNet-1k
validation set, which the dense model did not see. Relative to the held-out training images, top-1 accuracy on the official
validation set is 5.2–6.5 points lower for the fine-tuned networks and 7.2
points lower for the dense model. The relative performance of the training
rules follows the same pattern. ProbConv and zero-mask training are level at the mildest cut
( − 0.11 ± 0.18 -0.11\pm 0.18 at ρ = 0.9 \rho=0.9 ), and ProbConv leads by 4.69 points with 18 of 196
patches left ( Main Tab. 4 ). The spread over seeds is smaller than
on the development set at eight of the nine budgets, and compaction in
training stays below the zero mask at every budget.
Fine-tuned for the whole 30-epoch schedule at ToP-ViM’s setting (157/126),
ProbConv reaches 76.35 ± 0.18 % 76.35\pm 0.18\% , above the dense model ( 76.07 % 76.07\% ) and the 75.1 % 75.1\% that ToP-ViM reports for 30 epochs from the same checkpoint (three seeds;
ToP-ViM’s number averages several runs with
pruning after blocks 10 and 20, which removes 13.6% of the FLOPs in ToP-ViM’s convention with our
selector counted).
Compaction in training with ToP-ViM’s score stays 0.1–4.5 points below ProbConv at every budget.
The “ToP-ViM score” ranks tokens by the mean of the clipped SSM output, as
in ToP-ViM’s released code. During training, physical compaction uses this
score in place of our base score and omits the learned residual. Each budget
uses three seeds. At 69/24 patches, extending fine-tuning to 30 epochs narrows ProbConv’s lead from
3.7–4.0 to 1.9–2.0 points. ProbConv reaches 74.78 ± 0.03 % 74.78\pm 0.03\% , compared with 72.81 ± 0.12 % 72.81\pm 0.12\% for the zero mask and 72.88 ± 0.03 % 72.88\pm 0.03\% for compaction with
ToP-ViM’s score. It leads both methods in every seed.
At 69/24, we use one seed to vary the selector learning rate ( 10 − 4 10^{-4} or 10 − 3 10^{-3} instead of 3 ⋅ 10 − 4 3{\cdot}10^{-4} ) and the final LapSum temperature (0.1
or 0.5 instead of 0.25) separately for both training methods. The best final
temperature is 0.5 for both. Over three seeds at that temperature, ProbConv reaches 72.31 ± 0.04 % 72.31\pm 0.04\% and the zero mask 69.55 ± 0.22 % 69.55\pm 0.22\% (last block of Main Tab. 4 ). Tuning improves top-1 accuracy by 0.7 points for ProbConv and 1.7 points for the
zero mask. ProbConv still leads by 2.77 2.77 points on average, with paired gains of
2.56–3.04 points across seeds. The lead with the default settings is 3.72
points. With this setting at all nine
budgets, ProbConv leads the zero mask in every seed at every budget, by 2.93 to
0.18 points from the strongest to the mildest budget, including + 0.25 +0.25 at ρ = 0.9 \rho=0.9 , where the default settings tie ( − 0.11 -0.11 ); tuning helps the zero mask
most where it is weakest ( + 2.25 +2.25 at 59/18, against + 0.49 +0.49 for ProbConv).

Table 4 : At tight budgets, ProbConv’s advantage over zero-mask training carries
over to the official validation set. We evaluate Vim-Tiny with physical
compaction on 50,000 ImageNet-1k validation images and report top-1 accuracy
as mean ± \pm standard deviation over three seeds. The final block uses a
final LapSum temperature of 0.5 in place of 0.25, the best value at 69/24
patches. ProbConv leads at every tested budget with this temperature. Bold marks
the best fine-tuned result in each column of the main block.

Main Table 5 repeats the
comparison on Vim-Small [ 73 ] with the same short protocol,
selector and cuts, three seeds, at four budgets: 59/18, 69/24
and 98/49 patches (9.2, 12.2 and 25.0%, as for Vim-Tiny) and 109/61, which
removes 29.3% of the FLOPs with our selector counted, against 29.4% for the
Vim-S result of ToP-ViM [ 68 ] . The advantage carries over to Vim-Small. At all four tested budgets and in
every seed, ProbConv improves on zero-mask training, by 1.74 ± 0.25 1.74\pm 0.25 , 1.70 ± 0.27 1.70\pm 0.27 , 1.46 ± 0.58 1.46\pm 0.58 and 0.79 ± 0.47 0.79\pm 0.47 points from the strongest to
the mildest budget. As on Vim-Tiny, the lead grows
with compression, the zero mask scores 0.6–1.5 points higher with soft keep
values than after compaction, and ProbConv does not. At 12.2% the
larger network loses less against its dense model than Vim-Tiny (3.45 points
against 4.48). We report the validation set only: the Vim-S checkpoint has
seen the development images in training (93.02% dense top-1 on them).

blocks.en:
Main Table 7 changes one part of the
training signal at a time, with the protocol of Main Tab. 3 at all four
budgets. Its first three columns state whether training runs the deployed
compacted computation (binary keep values in the forward pass), which operator
carries the gradient to the selector through the convolution taps (ProbConv, the
zero mask or none), and whether the selector also receives a gradient through
the step gate.
The “soft forward” configuration uses the soft forward pass in all three
epochs. “Compaction in training” uses the fixed score and omits the learned
residual. Both DyVM configurations train our selector with DyVM’s rearranged
forward, which moves retained patches ahead of the masked, dropped patches.
Only the step-gated configuration also uses our step gating. Step gating matters most. Without it, ProbConv loses 0.20, 0.95, 2.12
and 7.18 points on the validation set from the mildest to the strongest
budget (seed-paired), and the zero mask loses a further 0.68–6.25 points.
Both deployed networks then fall up to 5.60 and 7.84 points below their
training forward. Stopping the gradient through the convolution leaves the forward pass
unchanged. On Vim, the resulting top-1 differences range from − 0.01 -0.01 to + 0.13 +0.13 points on validation and from − 0.24 -0.24 to + 0.24 +0.24 on development. Training
straight-through from the first step, without the soft epoch, costs 0.22 to
1.19 points against ProbConv (seed-paired means at the four budgets). With the
convolution gradient also blocked, the expectation enters neither the forward
pass nor the gradient: this variant is level with ProbConv at 69/24
( 71.55 ± 0.16 71.55\pm 0.16 against 71.59 ± 0.12 71.59\pm 0.12 ) but loses 1.23 ± 1.10 1.23\pm 1.10 , 1.19 ± 0.34 1.19\pm 0.34 and 0.15 ± 0.09 0.15\pm 0.09 points at 98/49, 118/71 and 147/111, in every seed at the
last two. On Vim the expectation in the convolution therefore helps through
the soft epoch, while the gradient through the taps adds nothing once that
epoch has run. How the selector
receives its gradient matters, however. DyVM’s rearranged forward also trains
the deployed computation but passes the gradient through masked convolution
taps; it stays 5.6 and 4.6 points below ProbConv at 69/24 and 98/49, and adding
step gating to it lowers it further at every budget (63.73, 67.15, 69.39 and
72.28 at the four budgets of Main Tab. 7 ; also 62.70 against
64.26 at 59/18 and 73.06 against 73.44 at 157/126). A soft
forward pass in all three epochs, never straight-through, is 0.33 and 0.34
points ahead of ProbConv at 147/111 and 118/71, level at 98/49 and 1.20 points
behind at 69/24, where its deployed network falls 2.46 points below its
training forward. The cost of training on a computation other than the
deployed one thus grows with compression, as for the zero mask. In summary,
ProbConv and its variant without the convolution gradient differ by at most 0.13
points at every budget; the variant adds a stop-gradient inside the operator,
so we keep the full operator as the default. ProbConv and its variant without the convolution gradient lead the comparison at
the two tightest budgets, 69/24 and 98/49 patches, the regime that compaction
targets. At 69/24, the other variants with step gating trail full ProbConv by
0.04 to 1.19 points, and the remaining training signals by 3.72 to 9.97
points.

three stages: after blocks 6, 12 and 18 the network keeps the fractions ρ \rho , ρ 2 \rho^{2} and ρ 3 \rho^{3} of the patch tokens, and the class token is
always kept. With ρ ∈ { 0.85 , 0.7 , 0.5 } \rho\in\{0.85,0.7,0.5\} this removes 20%, 36% and 52%

tokens, so the deployed network is the unmodified VideoMamba on a shorter
sequence; at ρ = 0.7 \rho=0.7 , blocks 7–12, 13–18 and 19–24 run on 1099, 769 and
539 tokens. The token norm rule scores tokens by the norm of the
residual stream; we evaluate it without training and after fine-tuning with
physical compaction, where only the backbone learns. The learned selector adds the output of a two-layer MLP, whose last

straight-through estimator and nested, exact-budget LapSum probabilities at
temperature 0.25 ( Sec. 2.3 ). It is trained

through ProbConv with step gating in both scan directions, the backward one on
the reversed sequence ( Sec. 2.2 ). At binary p p the latter computes
exactly the compacted network ( Proposition 2 ).

blocks.en:
All arms share the optimizer: AdamW with
learning rates 3 ⋅ 10 − 5 3{\cdot}10^{-5} for the backbone and 3 ⋅ 10 − 4 3{\cdot}10^{-4} for
the selector, weight decay 10 − 4 10^{-4} , a cosine schedule to 0.1 × 0.1\times after
warm-up, batch 32, drop path 0.1, label smoothing 0.1, and bfloat16 with ProbConv in float32. A training clip takes one random frame from each of 8 segments of
32 stored, uniformly spaced frames, with a random resized crop (area 25–100%)
and a horizontal flip. On Kinetics-400 [ 27 ] we fine-tune for
3 epochs (warm-up 0.3 epochs) on the 239,789 training clips available from
the CVDF mirror, with three seeds. We evaluate on 19,877 of the 19,906 validation videos with
VideoMamba’s 4 temporal × \times 3 spatial views and averaged softmax, where
the released model scores 76.65. On each of the three official splits of
HMDB51 [ 29 ] (3570 training and 1530 test videos) we first
fine-tune the dense model with a new head for 10 epochs, then each arm from it
for 5 epochs (warm-up 1 epoch) with three seeds. The seeds share
the test set of a split, whose binomial standard error is about 1.1 points. MACs are counted analytically per view (projections,
convolutions and scans of both directions, patch embedding and head); the dense
model has 12.15 GMACs. The FLOP counter of R-MeeTo [ 57 ] hooks
the projections, the convolution and the scan (as 9 ​ L ​ E ​ N + 2 ​ L ​ E 9LEN+2LE ) but counts only
one of the two scan directions of a block. On our forward pass, selector

blocks.en: 3.2 Frame selection in a convolutional video network
blocks.zh: 3.2 国家 革命视频网络中的帧选择

blocks.en:
OCSampler [ 35 ] selects N N of T T candidate frames in one step: a skim network, MobileNetV2 [ 54 ] with temporal shift [ 34 ] at 128 2 128^{2} , scores every candidate with a linear head, and a classifier runs on
the N N selected frames in temporal order. We use X3D-S [ 12 ] (Kinetics-400 weights, 160 2 160^{2} ) as the
classifier, with T = 10 T{=}10 and N = 4 N{=}4 , on ActivityNet-v1.3 [ 5 ] (10,014 of the 10,024 training and 4,916 of
the 4,926 validation videos), with the split files and the candidate
sampling of OCSampler: the video is cut into T T equal segments, and a
candidate is a random frame of its segment in training and the middle frame
at test time. X3D-S has no temporal stride, and its temporal convolutions are
depthwise, 5 × 1 × 1 5{\times}1{\times}1 in the stem and 3 × 3 × 3 3{\times}3{\times}3 in every
block. The selected frames form a compacted clip, so each temporal
convolution of the deployed classifier sees the neighbors that survive
selection, not the neighbors in the video.

blocks.en:
We apply the centered ProbConv of Main Eq. 9 to every temporal
convolution, with two taps on each side in the stem and one in every block. In
the squeeze-and-excitation units and the global pool, we weight each frame by
its keep probability. At binary
keep probabilities the outputs at the kept frames equal X3D-S on the
compacted clip, which we check numerically; at p ≡ 1 p\equiv 1 the network is the
dense X3D-S. BatchNorm uses its running statistics, so the dropped frames never
enter batch statistics. The zero-mask control multiplies the input of every
temporal convolution by the keep probabilities instead, so a kept frame sees
zeros where its neighbors were dropped.
blocks.zh:

blocks.en:
We follow the two stages of OCSampler. Stage I trains
X3D-S on N N random candidates in temporal order, i.e . , on the compacted clips
it will run, and the skim network on all T T candidates (SGD with Nesterov
momentum, batch 64, cosine schedule, 50 epochs, learning rates 0.005 0.005 and 0.01 0.01 ). Stage II freezes the classifier and trains the skim network and the
policy head for 50 epochs with the same optimizer. Every learned rule is
evaluated by the top- N N scores of its policy, with the classifier run dense
on the compacted clip and one center crop per video, and we report mAP of the
final checkpoint on the validation set. Hyperparameters are chosen on a fixed
subset of 1000 training videos, with both stages retrained on the remaining
ones: for every arm the learning rate in { 3 , 10 , 30 } ⋅ 10 − 4 \{3,10,30\}\cdot 10^{-4} , and
additionally τ ∈ { 0.3 , 1 , 3 } \tau\in\{0.3,1,3\} for top- N N ProbConv, η ∈ { 1 , η ∗ } \eta\in\{1,\eta^{*}\} for MuProp, and λ ∈ { 0.1 , 0.3 , 1 } \lambda\in\{0.1,0.3,1\} with the policy or LapSum
marginals for the sum. We then retrain each selected configuration on the full training set with
three seeds, and use the validation set only to report mAP.
Per video, X3D-S costs 0.31, 0.63 and 0.94 GFLOPs on 2, 4 and 6 frames and
1.56 on 10, and the skim network 1.02 GFLOPs on 10 frames at 128 2 128^{2} (fvcore).

Training through ProbConv on the masks that the policy
samples gives the best selection, 76.06 mAP against 75.59 for the
REINFORCE of OCSampler ( Main Tab. 11 ), and matches the released
OCSampler sampler on our classifier (75.98; with its own classifier and 6 frames, the released sampler reaches 75.74). Its lead over REINFORCE appears at every learning rate ( + 0.47 +0.47 , + 0.39 +0.39 and + 1.67 +1.67 at 3 3 , 10 10 and 30 ⋅ 10 − 4 30\cdot 10^{-4} , with the same seeds), in all three
seeds at the two larger rates and in two of three at the smallest. Sampled
ProbConv gives 76.06–76.18 mAP across the tested learning rates and 75.87–76.09
across the samplers at the learning rate of Main Tab. 13 . The same
ProbConv gradient at the top- N N mask is 0.99 points below REINFORCE, below it
in every seed and at every learning rate and temperature: the gradient
through the compacted network helps when it is taken on the masks the policy
draws, and a deterministic top- N N mask in training costs about 1.5 points.

mAP, 2.73 points above the zero mask at 71.87.

uniform rule, the largest gap in the table, so in this host the mismatch
between the trained and the deployed network matters more than the estimator.
The other learned rules gain 2.4–3.8 points over the uniform rule,
against the 7.1 points that separate it from all ten frames.

blocks.en: 3.3 Frame selection in Uni-AdaFocus
blocks.zh: 3.3 国家 在 Uni-AdaFocus 中选择框架

blocks.en:
Uni-AdaFocus [ 60 ] runs a cheap glance network on a coarse view of the whole video, and a learned
policy uses its features to choose the frames, and within them the patches,
that a large local network processes; the prediction is the sum of the
logits of both networks. We keep the temporal part of its X3D variant [ 12 ] and remove the spatial policy, the patches and the
early exit. From T 0 = 48 T_{0}{=}48 candidate frames per video (ActivityNet-v1.3, the
splits and candidate sampling of Main Sec. 3.2 , 160 2 160^{2} ), the
glance X3D-S sees T G = 16 T_{G}{=}16 , one per bin of three candidates. A temporal
convolution over its detached frame features scores the bins, and the
selector of Uni-AdaFocus turns the scores into K = 16 K{=}16 of the 48 candidates:
it reads the inverse of the cumulative distribution of the scores at K K stratified thresholds, interpolating linearly within bins (centered thresholds
at test time). The local X3D-L runs on the selected frames in temporal order, i.e . , on a compacted clip. Per video the glance network costs 2.50 and the
local network 4.82 GFLOPs (fvcore, without the policy network).

blocks.en:
The policy loss of Uni-AdaFocus, L temporal L_{\mathrm{temporal}} , is a Monte Carlo proxy on the frame logits of the
glance network: it weights them by draws from the softmax of the scores and
applies the cross-entropy. The local network, which runs on the selected
frames, gives the policy no signal. We add one: a policy pass of X3D-L
with ProbConv in every temporal convolution (as in Main Sec. 3.2 ) on all 48 candidates at keep values m + p − sg ⁡ ( p ) m+p-\operatorname{sg}(p) , where m m is the mask the selector drew and p p its marginals.
At binary keep values the pass computes X3D-L on the compacted clip
( Proposition 2 ), so its forward is the deployed network and only the
gradient flows to p p . The loss is the cross-entropy of the pass logits plus
the detached glance logits. The pass runs the local network in evaluation mode with frozen parameters, so
the dropped candidates never enter batch statistics and the networks train
identically in every arm. To limit memory use, the policy pass processes 8 of
the 32 videos in each batch. The linear interpolation of the
selector equals a piecewise constant density over the glance bins, which
gives the marginals over the 48 candidates; with collisions between
thresholds they are only approximately min ⁡ ( 1 , K ​ q ) \min(1,Kq) (error up to 0.075 for a
mild policy and 0.75 for a peaked one), so we also use exact-budget LapSum
marginals [ 59 ] with systematic sampling, whose marginals
are exact. Main Table 14 compares L temporal L_{\mathrm{temporal}} alone, REINFORCE
with the reward of OCSampler and the uniform clip as its baseline, and several

blocks.en:
All networks train together from the
Kinetics-400 weights with the losses of Uni-AdaFocus on the drawn compacted
clip: the cross-entropy of the summed logits and of the mean frame logits of
each network. We use the optimizer of the official Kinetics script, SGD with
momentum 0.9, learning rate 0.0025 0.0025 at batch 32 (0.005 at 64), scaled by 0.5
for the glance network and 0.4 for the policy, weight decay 5 ⋅ 10 − 5 5{\cdot}10^{-5} ,
gradient clipping at 20, dropout 0.5, a cosine schedule over 50 epochs with
one warm-up epoch, and bfloat16. We report the mAP of the final checkpoint
with centered thresholds and one center crop, and the same networks with a
flat policy (“uniform rule”), which separates what the policy adds at test
time from what training with it does to the networks. The ratio of the
policy learning rate is chosen per arm on the 1000 held-out training videos of Main Sec. 3.2 , from { 0.12 , 0.4 , 1.2 } \{0.12,0.4,1.2\} ; the hybrids keep the
official 0.4, and the weights of the policy pass are chosen on the same videos.
The chosen configuration is trained on the full training set with three
seeds.
The setting costs 7.32 GFLOPs per video.

blocks.en:
In our CUDA kernel, each warp processes one (batch, channel) row in tiles of
256 positions, eight per lane. The forward pass stores the rank- ( K − 1 ) (K{-}1) state at the start of each tile. The backward pass recomputes the state inside
each tile while running the reverse scan of Main Eq. 6 . Tap gradients are reduced
deterministically, inputs may be fp16 or bf16 with fp32 accumulation, and the
bias and SiLU are fused into the epilogue. The rank-one state also implements
the dechunker of Main Proposition 1 in fp32.

blocks.en: Appendix 7 Genomics: dynamic chunking in H-Net and LDARNet

blocks.en:
We train a one-stage H-Net [ 24 ] DNA language model on hg38
(14.8M parameters, 4096-base contexts, 20k steps) with the published routing,
dechunker and ratio loss towards N N bases per chunk, and sweep N N to compare
at matched compression. We fine-tune the released LDARNet-110M [ 30 ] on the 18 Nucleotide Transformer tasks [ 10 ] with the authors’ full protocol (ten folds, per-task
learning rates, early stopping; 540 runs) and on the nine Genomic Benchmarks [ 15 ] . In both hosts the baseline trains the router with
the published mechanism; our arms train it through ProbConv and step gating in
the main network and through the expected dechunker. Protocols are in Sec. 1 .

blocks.en:
Our run of the published fine-tuning reproduces the reported results (74.03
against 73.81 mean MCC), so we compare against the authors’ method at its
strength. Training the router through expected compaction raises the mean MCC
to 74.34 and improves 14 of the 18 tasks ( p = 0.009 p{=}0.009 over folds; Main Fig. 8 ), mostly splice
sites and enhancers, while histone marks and promoters change by at most 0.15;
the variant without the convolution gradient performs the same. Both ProbConv routers place more boundaries than the published one, but the gain
does not come from the extra chunks: with the pre-training ratio loss applied
to both routers, compression is similar (4.08 against 4.01 bases per chunk)
and ProbConv remains 0.25 points better ( p = 0.02 p{=}0.02 over folds), while the ratio
loss itself changes neither routing ( + 0.09 +0.09 and + 0.02 +0.02 ). The extra chunks leave inference time within 54–59 ms per batch of 64 on an
H100 for any compression between 3 and 6 bases per chunk. Controls with a
frozen router and with continued pre-training are in Sec. 9 . On
the nine Genomic Benchmarks, where our published-routing runs reproduce the
reported accuracies (88.30 against 88.48), the gains are small: + 0.21 +0.21 for
ProbConv ( p = 0.22 p{=}0.22 over folds) and + 0.14 +0.14 with more chunks without the
convolution gradient ( p = 0.01 p{=}0.01 ).

blocks.en:
With the forward pass fixed, the router or
selector receives gradients through the convolution taps, the step gate and
the dechunker. Stopping the convolution gradient changes little on LDARNet and Vim and costs
about one point in VideoMamba (0.2–0.5 in the replicate set; Main Tabs. 7 and 10 ). It improves H-Net
at matched compression. In speech, the effect depends on the encoder and decoding setup. For the
causal encoder, stopping the gradient changes WER by − 0.9 ± 1.5 -0.9\pm 1.5 points,
within the variation across seeds. It raises WER in the bidirectional encoder.
At the tighter budget without frame recovery, stopping the gradient lowers WER
by 6.3 points. Scaling the convolution gradient by λ \lambda produces monotone
trends on H-Net and in the bidirectional encoder
( Main Tabs. 24 and 21 ). In the
genomics and causal speech hosts the benefit thus comes from the exact
compacted forward pass and the gradients through the gated scan and the
expected dechunker. Cobra is the opposite case: without the convolution
gradient its selector falls 5.8 points below ProbConv, and without step gating it
loses nothing ( Main Tab. 35 ). The convolution gradient is
therefore host-dependent, from harmful on H-Net to decisive in Cobra.
REINFORCE on the exactly compacted network gives the best learned speech
selector and the weakest H-Net router in these comparisons. It trails ProbConv by
1.0 point in Cobra. This pattern is consistent with a greater role for the
pathwise gradient when many decisions share a sequence-level reward.

blocks.en:
LDARNet is also evaluated on the nine Genomic
Benchmarks tasks [ 15 ] , for which no fine-tuning code is
released. We follow its description: the protocol above with top-1 accuracy
for model selection and early stopping, its learning rates and batch sizes,
and sequences of up to 4096 bases ( Main Tab. 29 ). Our published-routing
runs reproduce the reported accuracies (88.30 against 88.48 on average; within
0.4 points on eight tasks and 1.8 below on the smallest, mouse enhancers with
242 test sequences). The gains here are small. The variant without the
convolution gradient improves 7 of 9 tasks ( + 0.14 +0.14 ; Wilcoxon p = 0.04 p{=}0.04 over
tasks, p = 0.01 p{=}0.01 over 90 folds), but it also keeps more chunks (3.27 against
3.88 bases per chunk). Full ProbConv compresses like the published routing (3.74)
and improves 5 of 9 tasks ( + 0.21 +0.21 , p = 0.22 p{=}0.22 over folds). Its mean rests on
the noisiest task ( + 2.2 +2.2 on mouse enhancers), and it is significantly better
on open chromatin ( + 0.36 +0.36 , at 3.94 against 3.53 bases per chunk) and on
coding sequences ( + 0.09 +0.09 ). Three tasks are close to saturation (above 95%).
With the learning rate of 10 − 3 10^{-3} of the regulatory task, the compression
varies widely across folds (published routing 1.5–23 bases per chunk, ProbConv 1.0–3.5), while the mean accuracies of the three routings differ by at most
0.06.

blocks.en: Appendix 10 Long-context language modeling: token selection in ReMamba

blocks.en:
ReMamba [ 66 ] adapts a Mamba-2.8B language
model [ 16 ] to long prompts by selective compression. A first pass
over the prompt yields last-layer hidden states; the leading fraction ϕ \phi of
the prompt ( p p in [ 66 ] ) forms a region of n n candidates,
each scored by the cosine similarity between a learned key of the candidate and
a learned query of the last prompt token, and the k = ⌈ ρ ​ n ⌉ k=\lceil\rho n\rceil highest-scoring candidates are kept. A second pass reads projections of the
kept states in place of the region, followed by the rest of the prompt, and
scales the step Δ \Delta of the kept states by their scores. The second pass
thus runs on a compacted sequence, and the selector learns only through the
scores of the candidates it already keeps. We follow the published fine-tuning:
LoRA of rank 32 for one epoch on 300k OpenOrca instructions [ 45 ] and 209k long instructions from OpenOrca and
LongAlpaca-12k [ 9 ] , truncated to 6000 tokens, with an
effective batch of 128 and a learning rate of 2 ⋅ 10 − 5 2{\cdot}10^{-5} . Prompts longer
than 1600 tokens draw ϕ ∼ U ⁡ ( 0.1 , 0.3 ) \phi\sim U(0.1,0.3) and ρ ∼ U ⁡ ( 0.05 , 0.2 ) \rho\sim U(0.05,0.2) per
example, with the same draw in every arm.

blocks.en:
We keep the first pass, the region, the scores and
the budget, and run the second pass on the uncompacted sequence with keep
probability p i p_{i} for candidate i i and one elsewhere. Every Mamba block of the
second pass uses ProbConv in place of its convolution and gates its step by p p ( Sec. 2.2 ), so that at binary p p the second pass is ReMamba’s compacted
one ( Proposition 2 ), and every candidate, kept or not, receives a gradient.
We train the selector with the soft forward pass ( Sec. 2.3 ): the
second pass uses the exact-budget LapSum probabilities, with a learned
temperature. A second series with the single cosine schedule trains ProbConv straight-through: the temperature decays log-linearly from 1 to 10 − 3 10^{-3} in
units of the score range of each example, and the straight-through gradient is
scaled by it, which keeps the gradient bounded as the selection sharpens. This
series includes a zero mask, with the same step gate and straight-through
training but ordinary convolutions on the masked inputs in place of ProbConv.
All arms are evaluated with ReMamba’s published compacted inference.

blocks.en:
We use the English LongBench-E [ 1 ] (13 tasks, 3668 examples) with the authors’ evaluation code: greedy decoding,
prompts truncated to 5500 tokens, ϕ = 0.18 \phi=0.18 and ρ = 0.009 \rho=0.009 . Rescoring the
authors’ released predictions reproduces their reported average of 27.86
exactly. The ReMamba paper specifies a cosine learning-rate schedule for its
single epoch [ 66 ] . The released multi-GPU script advances the scheduler once per process at each
optimizer step. The cosine length is set in optimizer steps, so the learning
rate completes a cycle every 1,989 of our 3,977 steps, or every 994 steps on
the authors’ eight GPUs. Our run ends at the peak learning rate. We read this as a side effect of multi-GPU training, not as the intended
schedule, and evaluate both versions. The published schedule uses the
released script as written, which lets us compare our reproduction with the
released adapter. The other setting uses the single cosine over the
epoch described in the paper. Each arm is trained once;
re-evaluating the same adapters in float32 changes the average by at most 0.2
points.
The task families are question answering (Qasper, MultiFieldQA, HotpotQA,
2WikiMQA), summarization (GovReport, MultiNews), few-shot learning (TREC,
TriviaQA, SAMSum), synthetic tasks (PassageCount, PassageRetrieval), and code
completion (LCC, RepoBench-P). As in LongBench-E, length buckets are based on
word counts.

The convolution matters in this host: with the same
step gate and straight-through training, a zero mask in place of ProbConv loses
1.21 points (27.12 to 25.91). The soft forward pass works in this host because training drives the keep
probabilities to the vertices. The keys and queries spread the cosine scores
about twentyfold, with little change in the learned temperature. By the end of
training, 97% of the keep mass lies on the top- k k candidates, so the soft
forward pass uses a selection close to the hard mask at inference.

Cobra’s Mamba blocks read in_proj.weight , dt_proj.weight and out_proj.weight directly, bypassing the
forward of a wrapper. Our LoRA module (rank 16) therefore exposes the merged
weight W + ( α / r ) ​ B ​ A W+(\alpha/r)BA as its weight , so that every call site and the

training-free rules to the dense model with LoRA. With LoRA, REINFORCE and RLOO
train the adapters with the ordinary gradient of the loss of the sampled
compacted network (RLOO: the mean over its four samples), while the selector
keeps its score-function gradient.

significantly different. Given its measured time, the zero-mask arms reach 58.4
and 57.9 and rearranged DyVM 54.7; REINFORCE, given the same time (3,777 steps),
reaches 60.4 and RLOO 60.5. Across all six time-matched comparisons, the gains on GQA, VQAv2 and POPE
remain significant in all three seed pairs. The six comparisons include three
at the scan budget and three at the measured kernel time
( Main Tab. 41 ). The TextVQA gain is significant in 17 of the 18
pairs. Main Figure 12 shows per-benchmark differences for four
further comparisons. The scores of ProbConv change little after 500 steps
( Main Tab. 37 ).

Main Table 35 separates the parts of the training signal; its two gradient columns state, as
in Main Tab. 7 , which operator carries the gradient through
the convolution taps and whether the step gate carries one. Without the gradient through the
convolution taps the forward pass is unchanged and reaches the vertices (soft
and hard held-out losses 0.773–0.806 and 0.772–0.806 at 10%, against
0.731–0.734 for ProbConv), but the selector is worse than the zero mask and
unstable: 54.2, 53.7 and 58.1 at 10%, 62.9, 61.6 and 58.7 at 25%, with
the losses on VQAv2 ( − 13.2 -13.2 ), POPE ( − 11.0 -11.0 ) and GQA ( − 7.9 -7.9 ), significant
in all three seed pairs at both budgets ( Main Tab. 41 ). The step
gate alone thus carries little information about which tokens to keep. Without
step gating the selector matches ProbConv (61.1, 61.1, 61.3 and 64.2, 64.5, 64.6;
within 1.2 points on every benchmark), although its training forward differs
from the deployed network (held-out loss 0.756–0.758 soft against
0.735–0.746 hard at 10%). With the compacted network, REINFORCE is below ProbConv on every seed: it scores
59.8–60.3 at 10%, compared with 61.0–61.3 for ProbConv, and 63.1–64.2 at
25%, compared with 64.2–64.4. The largest deficits are on POPE ( − 2.4 -2.4 ) and
VQAv2 ( − 2.2 -2.2 ), both significant in all three seed pairs at 10%. It is above
every other learned peer of Main Tab. 32 except its four-sample variant
RLOO. In Cobra the selector therefore learns from the gradient of
the expected compacted convolution; training on the deployed network is not
sufficient, and the exact scan is not necessary.

detail.
In the left example, none of the 46 retained patches overlaps the logo. The
vision encoder mixes information across the image before token selection. The 19 examples of Main Figs. 15 , 16 , 17 and 18 are fixed in advance: we take every 97th distinct image of POPE, TextVQA and
GQA in index order, at most eight per benchmark, with one question per image. For the 36 projector-level examples, the retained tokens extracted from the
language-model inputs match the displayed sets exactly, and the harness
reproduces the shown POPE probabilities within 0.016. For DTP, five of six
examples match. An occlusion test confirms the patch geometry (the
bottom 6-pixel strip of the image changes no token). Main Figure 14 counts how often each position is kept: ProbConv spreads its budget over the
image, the zero-mask arm concentrates on the last raster positions, the Δ \Delta score and DTP always keep the first token, and DyVM keeps a fixed
cluster at the bottom left, a SigLIP artifact ( Sec. 12 ). Section 12 also tests why the selector of ProbConv works: its gradient, its training dynamics and what its tokens cover.

blocks.en:
As in ReMamba ( Sec. 10 ), the soft
forward pass works here because training drives it to the vertices, where it
is the deployed compacted network. With the annealed soft forward at 10% of the language model’s FLOPs, stopping
the convolution gradient lowers the mean from 61.1 to 55.3, while removing
step gating gives 61.2. With a straight-through forward, both paths matter:
the full model scores 60.6, compared with 50.3 and 50.4 when the convolution
gradient or the step gate is removed ( Main Tab. 35 ). Relative to matched zero-mask training at 10%, the largest gains are on VQAv2
( + 6.3 +6.3 ), POPE ( + 5.8 +5.8 ) and GQA ( + 4.2 +4.2 ). TextVQA gains 0.7 points against
this control and 7.7 against the Δ \Delta score of layer 0. VSR and VizWiz
show little consistent benefit. With the same LoRA setup for every rule, ProbConv gives the highest mean at both
budgets (61.7 and 64.2). Four-sample RLOO is within 0.2 points (61.5 and
64.1). The layer-0 Δ \Delta score gives 60.1 and 63.2. At batch size 1 on a GH200 the end-to-end time is
dominated by the vision encoder and kernel launches (prefill 82–90 ms for
every rule), so pruning the visual span saves little wall-clock time there. On
an H100 (bf16 prefill of the vision encoder, projector, selector and language
model, synthetic images), the prefill takes 66.0 ms for the dense model and
35.5 and 34.8 ms at 25% and 10% of the language model’s FLOPs at batch
size 1. At batch size 32 the compacted networks process 111.9 and 140.9 images per
second against 49.5 for the dense model ( 2.26 × 2.26\times and 2.84 × 2.84\times ), and the
selector costs no more than the Δ \Delta rule (110.0 and 137.7 images per second).

blocks.en: Appendix 12 Vision–language: what the Cobra selectors learn

blocks.en:
The short convolution in Cobra mixes a retained token with the three preceding
survivors. At 46 of 729 visual tokens, these neighbors can be far apart in
raster order. Across 500 POPE images, the deployed distance distribution has a
peak at 27 positions, one image row. ProbConv already approximates this
distribution after 500 training steps, while the zero-mask convolution reads
only the three original predecessor offsets ( Main Fig. 23 ). We
also examine the gradients of the training computations, the evolution of the
keep probabilities and what the kept tokens cover. Unless noted otherwise, the
diagnostics use seed 0 of the frozen-backbone rules at 10% of the FLOPs
( k = 46 k=46 of 729 tokens) and the first 500 distinct POPE images; each diagnostic
states the number of questions or images it uses. The learned rules are read at their checkpoints
after 500, 1,000, 1,500 and 2,000 steps. Because the visual tokens precede the
text, every selector score depends on the image only.

For each

instances of the asked category onto the 27 × 27 27{\times}27 token grid, as Cobra
sees the image, and measure which share of the object area each rule keeps
( Main Fig. 22 ). At 46 tokens DyVM keeps the most (27.1%),
followed by the zero-mask convolution (20.6%), ProbConv (17.3%), the zero mask
(16.9%), DTP (15.8%), the Δ \Delta score (13.4%) and uniform selection
(5.9%; random 6.3%). Coverage alone thus does not explain the ranking of Main Tab. 34 . What differs is how useful the kept part is to
the language model: when at least one kept token lies mostly ( ≥ 50 % \geq 50\% ) on the
object, ProbConv answers 83.3% of these questions correctly, against 74.8% for
DyVM, 77.4% for the zero-mask convolution, 66.6% for the zero mask, 78.8% for
the Δ \Delta score, 75.7% for DTP and 74.1% for uniform selection; when no
kept token does, every rule is at 15–23%. This is consistent with a selector
that is trained through the network it is deployed in and therefore picks the
tokens that network can use, rather than the largest share of the object. We measure this association on the “yes” half of POPE for one seed. The
questions that satisfy the overlap condition vary across rules.

Each Mamba block of Cobra has a
causal convolution with K = 4 K=4 , so a kept token mixes with the three tokens
before it in the compacted sequence, which can lie far back in raster
order. During training, ProbConv replaces the convolution by its expectation over
the compactions: the m m -th tap reads token j j with the probability that j j is the m m -th kept token before t t . The zero-mask convolution instead reads
the raw neighbours t − 1 , … , t − 3 t-1,\dots,t-3 , most of them zeroed
( Main Fig. 23 ). Over all 500 images and the kept tokens of the
final selector, the distance at which the deployed network reads extends
far beyond the three raw neighbours, with a peak at 27, the token directly
above in the image. The expected window of ProbConv already matches this
distribution after 500 steps, while the zero-mask convolution trains only on
distances 1–3.
